lead: Software is more than code: it is programs, data and documents, and the kind of software decides how it is engineered. A meter's firmware, a bank's payroll and a UPI payment library are all software, yet each needs a different approach. This chapter defines software, contrasts it with hardware, lists the application domains, defines legacy software and corrects six common myths. Without this base, process models look like arbitrary ceremony; with it, each model is a sensible answer to a particular kind of product.
prereq: Nothing; this opens the unit. The process models that follow are introduced in 1.4.

sections.h3: Software is programs, data and documents

blocks.text: Software is the collection of programs, data and documents that makes a computer useful. A program is a set of instructions. Data is everything the program reads or writes: a customer table, a settings file, a saved invoice. Documents describe the software: the requirement note, the design sketch, test cases, the user manual. Delete the documents and the program still runs, but nobody can change it safely. That is why the definition has three parts, not one.

Software is developed, not manufactured. A factory makes identical hardware units and the cost per unit falls as volume rises. Software is built once, at the cost of people's time, and each further copy costs almost nothing.

Hardware wears out from heat, dust and vibration, so its failure rate follows a bathtub curve: high at the start, low in the middle, high at the end. Software does not wear out; it deteriorates. Every change risks breaking something that worked, so the failure rate climbs with each modification unless the code is cleaned up. The cause is change, not use.

Software resembles other engineering products in the work it demands: requirements, design, review, estimation, standards and client acceptance apply to a bridge and to a payroll system alike. It differs in being intangible, having no spare parts and no manufacturing tolerance, being copied in seconds, and carrying almost all its cost in human effort rather than material.

sections.h3: Changing role, application domains and legacy software

blocks.text: The role of software has shifted. Custom code for one client on one machine has given way to four shapes. Product lines: one core sold to many customers by configuration. Software as a service: the customer pays a subscription and uses the vendor's running system, like a GST filing portal billed per return. Embedded systems: software inside a device, such as the firmware of an electricity meter. AI-enabled systems: behaviour learned from data, used in fraud checks and recommendations. Each shape pushes engineering a different way — reuse and configuration for product lines, timing and memory discipline for embedded, data and model quality for AI.
Application domains group software by who uses it and what it must do:

items: System software: operating systems, compilers, device drivers, file systems. It serves other software, not the end user directly.
Application software: payroll, inventory, booking, results portals. Web and mobile apps are the largest modern sub-class.
Engineering and scientific software: CAD, circuit simulation, weather and structural models; heavy floating-point computation.
Embedded software: firmware inside a device, reading sensors and driving actuators under real-time limits.
Product-line and reuse software: libraries, frameworks and components reused across products, such as a payment SDK.
Web and mobile applications: network-facing, many users and devices, short release cycles.
Artificial intelligence software: prediction and recommendation learned from data instead of written by hand.

blocks.text: Legacy software is old software still in production and still business-critical. Ten or twenty years old, it runs on an outdated platform or language, few engineers understand it, the documentation is incomplete, and every change is risky. Organisations keep it because it works, it encodes years of business rules, and replacing it costs and risks more than maintaining it. A bank's core ledger is the usual example. The options are to wrap it, re-engineer it, or replace it phase by phase (see Unit 6, Software maintenance and re-engineering).

A myth is a belief that sounds obviously true and is false. Software myths survive because they excuse a shortcut already taken. They come from three groups: management, the customer, and the practitioner.

head: Group and myth
Reality
rows: Management: adding programmers catches up a late project
Late additions add communication paths and training load; the project slips further.
Management: a general statement of the objective is enough to start coding
Missing requirements surface later as rework, the costliest kind to fix.
Customer: requirements will keep changing, and change is easy
Change is easy to request and costly to absorb; each change must be evaluated and tracked.
Customer: a working program is the whole product
The product also needs documents, test records and training material to be usable and maintainable.
Practitioner: once the program runs, the job is done
Maintenance begins at first delivery and lasts for most of the product's life.
Practitioner: the only deliverable is working code
Design records, test cases and user documents are deliverables too.

blocks.text: Myths cost marks in two ways. A student who writes only the myth has answered half the question; the correction carries the marks. A team that believes a myth skips the work the myth denies — reviews, documents, change control — and pays for it later as rework.

spec.aria: A tree splits 40 applications into 25 application and web, 8 embedded, 5 product-line and reuse, and 2 legacy applications.

examples.question: A Chennai IT firm maintains 40 applications: 25 custom web apps for clients, 8 embedded firmware products for meter makers, 5 reusable payment libraries, and 2 payroll systems that are 12 years old. (a) Classify all 40 into application domains. (b) Identify the legacy systems. (c) The 2 payroll systems are maintained by 5 engineers, and the manager adds 3 more to catch up. Using communication paths n(n−1)/2 for a team of n people, compute the paths before and after, and state whether the myth 'adding programmers catches up a late project' holds.
steps: Check the inventory: 25 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 40. Nothing is left unclassified.
The 25 custom web apps serve end users over a network: application software, web sub-domain.
The 8 firmware products run inside a meter and talk to hardware: embedded software.
The 5 payment libraries are built once and reused across products: product-line and reuse software.
The 2 payroll systems are 12 years old, still in production and still business-critical: legacy software.
Extra paths = 28 − 10 = 18. Each path must be kept in sync, and the 3 new engineers need training on code they did not write.
The myth fails: the late project gains 18 communication paths and loses senior time to mentoring, so it usually finishes even later.
examples.answer: 25 application/web, 8 embedded, 5 product-line/reuse and 2 legacy applications, 40 in total; the payroll team's communication paths grow from 10 to 28, an extra 18, so adding programmers does not catch up a late project.

traps: Writing 'software = program'. Software is programs plus data plus documents; the documents are what make maintenance possible.
Calling any old program legacy. Legacy means old software still in production and still business-critical; an unused program from two years ago is dead code, not legacy.
Saying software wears out. Hardware wears out; software deteriorates because of change.
Listing a myth without the correction. The marks are for the corrected reality, stated in one line.
Confusing 'developed, not manufactured' with 'free to produce'. Copying the second unit is nearly free; building the first one is not.

quiz.q: Define software in one sentence and name its three parts.
quiz.a: Software is the collection of programs, data and documents that makes a computer useful; the parts are programs (instructions), data (what the program reads and writes) and documents (requirements, design, test cases, manuals).

quiz.q: Name four application domains of software.
quiz.a: Any four of: system software, application software, engineering and scientific software, embedded software, product-line and reuse software, web and mobile applications, artificial intelligence software, legacy software.

quiz.q: Software does not wear out, yet its failure rate rises over time. Explain why.
quiz.a: Hardware fails through physical wear such as heat and dust. Software fails through change: each modification can break something that worked, defects accumulate, and documents drift away from the code. So the failure rate climbs with each round of maintenance unless the code is refactored.

quiz.q: Give one difference between system software and application software, with an example of each.
quiz.a: System software serves other software, for example an operating system or a compiler; application software serves the end user's task, for example a payroll package or a railway booking app.

quiz.q: A firm has 60 applications: 30 web apps, 12 embedded firmware, 10 reusable libraries and 8 systems over 15 years old that run the accounts. Classify them by domain and state the total.
quiz.a: 30 application/web, 12 embedded, 10 product-line and reuse, 8 legacy; 30 + 12 + 10 + 8 = 60, so all are classified.

quiz.q: A late project has 6 engineers. The manager adds 4. Compute the communication paths n(n−1)/2 before and after, and decide whether the myth holds.
quiz.a: Before: n = 6, paths = 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15. After: n = 10, paths = 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45. Extra = 30 paths. The myth fails: 30 new channels plus training for 4 newcomers slow the team, so the project usually finishes later.

quiz.q: Why do organisations keep legacy software instead of replacing it at once?
quiz.a: It still works and still carries business rules built over years. Replacing it means re-deriving undocumented rules, retraining users and risking a critical service. So the cheaper path is often to wrap or re-engineer it in phases.

quiz.q: State the myth 'we have a general objective, so we can start coding' and correct it in one line.
quiz.a: Myth: a general statement of the objective is enough to begin. Reality: unclear requirements reappear as rework, the costliest kind of change.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now treats software supply chains and open-source licences as a domain of their own, because a product may be mostly third-party components. Machine learning has made data a first-class engineering artefact, so 'software plus documents' is often extended to 'software, data, documents and trained models'. Regulated sectors keep legacy systems alive for decades, which is why wrapping and re-engineering are steady jobs.
